messages.subject: dplyr: Joining Different tbls
messages.body_plain:

Thanks!
M

messages.subject: Re: dplyr: Joining Different tbls

Yes. But you'll need to set copy = TRUE because it will send the rhs table to the lhs, which is potentially expensive.
Hadley

messages.subject: summarise - plyr vs. dplyr
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I spent a little while to see if this had been addressed already here - I didn't see anything, so apologies in advance if it is elsewhere.

I managed to stumble (and fall) across a big difference between the summarise in dplyr and summarise in plyr. Using dplyr, summarize expects that for each group there will be returned a single row. plyr makes no such expectation.

This is fine, I have no problem with that.

Here is something I could do using plyr:

mtcars_slim <- summarise(mtcars, mpg_per_cyl = mpg / cyl)

Using dplyr, here's my best first guess:

mtcars_slim <-
  mtcars %.%
  mutate(mpg_per_cyl = mpg/cyl) %.%
  select(mpg_per_cyl)

If I have, for example, twenty variables to mutate/select, this can get a bit heavy and introduce more opportunity for typos.

Is there (or could there be) a way to do this more succinctly?

Thanks,

Ian

messages.subject_clean: Adapting dplyr for more programmatic use?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have a large dataset that I'd like to summarize and plot several different ways.  I currently do this by importing the data into sqlite and then paste()ing together SQL queries inside a function.  I was very hopeful that I could replace the nasty code that assembles SQL queries with some very pleasant and readable dplyr code.  But it appears that dplyr in it's current form isn't really meant for this purpose.  Rather, it's primarily intended for interactive use.  To illustrate what I'm up to:

library(dplyr)
data<-tbl_df(data.frame(class1 = sample(letters, 50, replace=T),
    class2 = sample(letters, 50, replace=T),
    value = runif(50)))

# Both of these work
group_by(data, class1) %.% summarise(n=n())
group_by(data, "class1") %.% summarise(n=n())

# This does not
rollup<-function(data_tbl, column) {
    group_by(data, column) %.% summarise(n=n())
}
rollup(data, "class1")
rollup(data, "class2")

Of course, my real rollup() function is substantially more complex.

There was a thread not too long ago when Hadley suggested a workaround as below, and said that dealing with this issue was on his long-term roadmap for dplyr.

# This does work
column <- "class1"
eval(substitute(group_by(data, column),
    list(column=as.name <http://as.name>(column)))) %.% summarise(n=n())

My question is whether there isn't some simple 90% solution to my problem.  My R meta-programming skills are feeble, but I wonder whether I could write something vaguely akin to aes_string() from ggplot2 that would wrap group_by().  This 90% solution wouldn't have be to good enough to bake into the dplyr codebase, but could make the workaround above much more concise.

Is what I'm after possible?  Reasonable?  Any help would be appreciated.

Thanks!

-J

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

For this specific case, dplyr does already provide a version of
group_by that doesn't do any special evaluation: regroup.  It's not
terribly well documented, but you need to pass it a list of symbols.
There's a few way to get that list depending on what your input is:

library(dplyr)

# As a bare variable
rollup <- function(tbl, column) {
  cols <- list(substitute(column))
  tbl %.% regroup(cols) %.% summarise(n = n())
}
mtcars %.% rollup(cyl)

# Multiple variables
rollup <- function(tbl, ...) {
  cols <- dots(...)
  tbl %.% regroup(cols) %.% summarise(n = n())
}
mtcars %.% rollup(vs, am)

# As a string:
rollup <- function(tbl, column) {
  cols <- list(as.name <http://as.name>(column))
  tbl %.% regroup(cols) %.% summarise(n = n())
}
mtcars %.% rollup("vs")

If you'd like to learn more metaprogramming, I'd recommend
http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Computing-on-the-language.html and
http://adv-r.had.co.nz/Expressions.html

Hadley

library(plyr)

             total = sum(total))

three <- Batting %.%
         group_by(playerID, yearID, teamID) %.%
         summarise(total = sum(G))

four  <- three %.%
         group_by(yearID) %.%
         summarise(total = sum(total))

Can anyone tell me why data frames two and four end up differently?

Thank you,

Jake

messages.subject: Best practices for handling metadata and large datasets?
messages.subject_clean: Best practices for handling metadata and large datasets?
messages.body_plain:
I often find myself working with data that includes metadata (a small dataframe that is short and somewhat wide) and much bigger numerical data (a very long skinny dataframe) and would love to hear opinions about best practices for working with this sort of data.

An example could be: I have 200 subjects who have been wearing one of three heart rate monitoring devices that records their heart rate once each minute for weeks, and a temperature monitoring device that records their temperature once every 30 minutes during the same time period.  It's a crossover design where each subject wears each of the three HR monitoring devices during different time periods.

So I have a dataframe hrDf with all the heart rates for all subjects, with columns Subject, DateTime, and HeartRate -- very long, very skinny.  Similarly, I have a dataframe tempDf with all the temperatures for subjects, with columns Subject, DateTime, and HeartRate -- also quite long, and very skinny.  Then I have metadata in a dataframe metaDf that has columns Subject, Age, Weight, Height, BPTreatment, StartDate, DeviceType, etc.  that records information for each subject -- this will have at least 3 rows per subject, often more to record various events -- let's say 3-12 rows per subject, and 12-50 columns.  So, wide and short.

In the course of analysis I generally will be applying a variety of functions to the long skinny dataframes, some but not all of which depend on information in the metadata.  I've done this different ways.  Sometime I merge portions of the metadata into the long skinny dataframes (for instance DeviceType). Sometimes I use ddply to operate on metaDf, but pass hrDf or tempDf to the function.  Sometimes I keep things like hrDf and tempDf separate, sometimes I merge them together.  I've used various approaches somewhat haphazardly, sometimes based on the size of the data and computational considerations, sometimes not.

I haven't settled on "best practices" for this type of process, but I'm embarking on a large and complex project that will involve lots of this type of data and would like to decide on an approach.  Since I assume others often work with data of this general form, I'd love to hear suggestions.  Note: I'm just getting started with dplyr, which I assume will replace my use of ddply.

-Elaine
